name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
info: In November 636 the army of the Rashidun Caliphate defeated the Sasanian army of Rustam Farrokhzad at al-Qadisiyyah in Iraq, after which Ctesiphon fell and the Sasanians lost Mesopotamia.

facts.date: November 636; the advance is widely believed to have begun on 16 November 636 and the fighting is told over four days, with a final day on which Rustam was killed
facts.place: Al-Qadisiyyah, on the west bank of the river Ateeq, a branch of the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq; in 2024 researchers identified the likely site as an open field about 19 kilometres (12 miles) south of modern Kufa
facts.sides: The Rashidun Caliphate under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, about 30,000 men including 7,000 cavalry, rising to 36,000 with the Syrian contingent and local Arab allies; the Sasanian Empire under Rustam Farrokhzad, about 60,000 in one account, while modern estimates suggest about 30,000 on each side, though most scholars agree the Sasanians outnumbered the Muslims by a sizable margin
facts.outcome: The Rashidun army won after Rustam was killed and the Sasanian line collapsed. The Sasanians lost Mesopotamia, and Ctesiphon was taken in March 637.

t: The fighting is told over four days, with a final day on which Rustam Farrokhzad was killed, and the Sasanian line collapsed after his death.
Accounts of how Rustam died differ: one is dismissed as unlikely for its literary devices and inconsistencies, and another is likely an invention of later story-tellers.
The defeat left the Sasanians unable to defend against the Rashidun siege of Ctesiphon, which fell in March 637; the Sasanian Empire was annexed by 651.
dyk: In 2024 researchers from Durham University and the University of al-Qadisiyyah used declassified American spy satellite imagery and texts describing the Darb Zubaydah, a pilgrimage road, to identify the likely battlefield.
ev: Khalid ibn al-Walid wins a series of battles in Iraq and takes Al-Hirah
Abu Bakr dies and Umar ibn al-Khattab becomes caliph; the Muslims are defeated at the Battle of the Bridge
The Sasanian and Rashidun armies camp at al-Qadisiyyah
The Byzantine army is defeated at the Battle of Yarmouk
The Sasanian army crosses the Ateeq and the first day of fighting begins
Rustam is killed, the Sasanian front collapses and the Muslims are victorious
Ctesiphon is taken after a siege of two months

sections.background:
After Muhammad's death, Abu Bakr established control over Arabia through the Ridda Wars and then launched campaigns against Syria and Palestine. In Iraq a volunteer army under Khalid ibn al-Walid won a series of battles in 633 and took the capital of Iraq, Al-Hirah, in the last week of May. Abu Bakr died in August 634 and was succeeded by Umar ibn al-Khattab. Khalid was sent west with half his army, and the Muslim forces left in Iraq were too few to hold the region. Abu Ubaid, sent from Madinah, was defeated and killed at the Battle of the Bridge, and Muthanna withdrew the remnant, about 3,000 strong, across the Euphrates.

The Sasanian Empire had been weakened by the war with the Byzantine Empire of 602 to 628 and by a civil war. Yazdegerd III became emperor at the age of eight in 632, and real power lay with the generals Rustam Farrokhzad and Piruz Khosrow. In 635 he sought an alliance with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius and ordered large armies to gather to reclaim Iraq. The plan was to be a coordinated attack, but when Heraclius began his offensive in May 636 Yazdegerd could not coordinate in time. Umar allegedly knew of the alliance and chose to finish the Byzantines first. The Byzantine army was defeated at Yarmouk in August 636, three months before al-Qadisiyyah.
sections.forces:
Umar raised new armies from throughout Arabia and appointed Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, a member of the Quraysh, to command. Because of Sa'd's inexperience Umar told him to seek the advice of experienced commanders. The army was a volunteer force of newly recruited contingents, and Umar lifted the ban on the former apostate tribes taking part. Sa'd, who suffered from sciatica and boils, directed the battle from the old royal palace through his deputy Khalid ibn Urfuta. The infantry stood in four corps about 150 metres apart, each with a cavalry regiment at the rear. The army numbered about 30,000, including 7,000 cavalry, and rose to 36,000 with the Syrian contingent and local Arab allies. A force of 5,000 veterans of Yarmouk arrived on the second day.

The Sasanian army, under Rustam, was in camps on the east bank of the Ateeq, with a bridge as the only crossing. In one account it numbered about 60,000: 45,000 infantry in four divisions, 15,000 cavalry held as a reserve and about 33 elephants, eight with each division, on a front of about 4 kilometres. Hormuzan, Jalinus, Piruzan and Mihran held its wings, right centre and rear. Modern estimates, drawn from the logistics of the two sides, suggest about 30,000 on each side, but most scholars agree that the Sasanians and their allies outnumbered the Muslims by a sizable margin.
sections.course:
For three months the sides negotiated. Muslim emissaries invited Yazdegerd to convert or pay the jizya, and Rustam, inclined to avoid fighting, offered the Arabs gifts to leave. The talks failed. On 16 November 636 Rustam had a canal converted into a road and the Sasanian army crossed it before dawn, facing southwest with the river behind it. Duels opened the battle. The Sasanian left wing attacked first, and elephants led the charge on both sides of the field, driving back the Muslim right and left. The Muslims answered with counterattacks, and on the left Asim ibn Amr had his archers shoot the men on the elephants while the infantry cut the saddle girths. The fighting ended at dusk, inconclusive, with heavy losses on both sides.

On 17 November the Syrian advance guard under al-Qa'qa ibn Amr arrived at noon, sending its men in small groups to suggest a larger force. There were no elephants that day, and the Sasanians repulsed repeated attacks. On 18 November Rustam sent the elephant corps forward again and tried to seize the palace where Sa'd sat, but a Muslim cavalry contingent drove his regiment away. The Muslims blinded the elephants and cut off their trunks until they fled through the Sasanian ranks. The fighting went on through the night and on 19 November Qa'qa's men pierced the Sasanian centre.

On the final day, in a sandstorm, Rustam was killed. The Sasanians, not knowing of his death at first, fought on. Their front finally collapsed, and Jalinus took command of the remainder and got the bulk of the army across the bridge.
sections.aftermath:
Sa'd sent the cavalry in several directions after the fleeing Persians. Stragglers they met were killed or taken captive, and the Sasanians suffered heavy casualties in the pursuit. The Arabs gained large spoils, among them the jewel-encrusted royal standard, the Darafsh-i Kawiyan. Its jewel was cut up and sold in pieces in Medina. Sa'd sent word of the victory to Umar.

The battle shook Sasanian rule in Iraq to its foundations but did not end it in Mesopotamia, since as long as the Sasanians held Ctesiphon they could try to recover what they had lost. Umar therefore ordered the Muslims to push on to the capital. The siege of Ctesiphon lasted two months and the city was taken in March 637, after which Muslim forces conquered the Persian provinces up to Khuzistan. A drought in Arabia in 638 and the plague of Imwas in 639 slowed the conquest. Umar is reported to have wished for a mountain of fire between the Muslims and the Persians.

The Sasanians continued the struggle to regain the lost land, and a Persian counterattack was repulsed at Nahavand in December 641. Umar then planned a full-scale invasion of the Sasanian Empire. Yazdegerd III was killed in 651, in the reign of the caliph Uthman, which ended the Sasanian line and empire.
sections.sources:
The course of the battle comes largely from the Muslim chronicles, which record several duels between champions of the two sides and give the days names. The chronicles tell the death of Rustam in different ways. In one, Hilal ibn Ullafah cut the girdle of a load of weapons on a camel behind which Rustam sheltered from the sandstorm, and the weapons broke his back before Hilal beheaded him; this has been dismissed as unlikely, because of suspicious literary devices and inconsistencies in the story. A version from Ya'qubi says that four men found the body. A third, in which Sa'd killed Rustam in single combat while Rustam was blinded by the sandstorm, is likely an invention of later story-tellers.

Other episodes are doubtful: the alliance between Yazdegerd and Heraclius is only alleged, as is Rustam's rebuke of Yazdegerd over the basket of earth. The numbers are modern estimates from logistics, and most scholars hold that the Sasanians were the larger force. In 2024 scholars from Durham University and the University of al-Qadisiyyah identified the likely site, using declassified American spy satellite imagery and historical texts describing the Darb Zubaydah.
sections.legacy:
The battle is considered one of the most significant engagements of the Muslim conquest of Persia and, with it, of the early Muslim conquests as a whole. It left the Sasanian army unable to defend against the siege of Ctesiphon and forced it to retreat from all of Mesopotamia. This opened the way to later offensives into the Persian mainland, including the battles of Jalula and Nahavand, and the Sasanian Empire was annexed by 651.

The battle shook Sasanian rule in Iraq, and its memory was kept in the names of the days. The Muslim chronicles call the first day Yawm al-Armath, the Day of Disorder, the third day Yaum-ul-Amas and the night that followed the Night of Rumbling Noises.

The Arab fighters became known as Ahl al-Qadisiyyah, or Ahl al-Qawadis, and held the highest prestige among later Arab settlers in Iraq and in its garrison town of Kufa. Umar, after the conquests that followed, wanted a break to manage the conquered territories and wished to leave the rest of Persia to the Persians, but later planned a full-scale invasion of the empire he regarded as his arch-rival.

The Persian view of the defeat was the opposite: one of great embarrassment, humiliation and scorn. The pride of the imperial Sasanians had been hurt by the Arab conquest of Iraq, and they sought to regain the lost territory.

summary: At al-Qadisiyyah in November 636 the Rashidun army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas defeated the Sasanian army of Rustam Farrokhzad, who was killed in the fighting. Ctesiphon fell in March 637, and the Sasanian Empire was annexed by 651.
references: Parvenah Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia: The Rise and Fall of an Empire (I.B. Tauris, 2014)
Peter Crawford, The War of the Three Gods: Romans, Persians and the Rise of Islam (Pen and Sword, 2013)
notes: The article gives two Sasanian strengths: about 60,000 (45,000 infantry plus 15,000 cavalry) and a modern estimate of about 30,000 on each side; both are given. No casualty figures are given anywhere.
Place: the article says the town lay 30 miles from Kufah in one place and the 2024 site is about 19 km south of Kufa in another; I used the 2024 figure only for the site.
Article is thin on sources: it names no historian except Ya'qubi and al-Tabari in passing; the sources section is built from its hedges on Rustam's death, the alliance and the basket story.

The article's section on Rustam's death says 'Qa'qa and his men dashed toward the Sasanian headquarters. Meanwhile ... Rustam was found dead with over 5 wounds'; I gave the sandstorm only. Also the article calls the 'Al-Tabari' version likely an invention; I wrote the single combat version without naming al-Tabari.

Article says Day 4 was 19 November and the 'final day' is separate; the dates of the final day are not given, so the ev entry for 19 November follows the Day 4 heading and the profile says the fighting is told over four days with a final day. Editor to check.
The article names 'Hormuzan, Jalinus, Piruzan, Mihran' as wing commanders; the lead says the advance began 16 November, 'widely believed'.

Article's lead calls the victory 'decisive' and 'cataclysmic'; I kept 'considered one of the most significant'. Left out: troop equipment, Muslim chronicle quotations by Rustam and Rabi bin Amir, the Qa'qa camouflaged camels, Maharbal-type anecdotes.
Article says Heraclius's army was 'annihilated' at Yarmouk; I wrote 'defeated'.
